title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (Core Excerpts)
author: Frederick Douglass
source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, Written by Himself (1845)
citation: Douglass, Frederick. Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, Written by Himself. Anti-Slavery Office, Boston, 1845.

sections.heading: Chapter 6: Literacy as the Pathway to Freedom

epigraph.quote: From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
epigraph.attribution: —Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass

paragraphs: Sent to Baltimore as a young boy to serve Hugh and Sophia Auld, Frederick experienced a turning point in his life. Mrs. Auld, who had never owned a slave before, began teaching him the alphabet and how to spell simple words. When Mr. Auld discovered this, he severely forbade it, warning that teaching a slave to read would spoil him forever and make him discontented and unmanageable.

Mr. Auld's bitter opposition became Douglass's greatest enlightenment: 'It was a new and special revelation, explaining to me the white man's power to enslave the black man... From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.' Douglass resolved at whatever cost to learn to read. He carried bread to poor white street boys in Baltimore, trading crusts of bread for spelling lessons on the sidewalks, and secretly copied letters from shipyard cargo boards.

sections.heading: Chapter 10: The Battle with Mr. Covey and The Rebirth of a Free Spirit

epigraph.quote: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
epigraph.attribution: —Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass

paragraphs: At sixteen, Douglass was rented out to Edward Covey, a notorious 'slave breaker' known for breaking the spirit of defiant young men. For six months, under relentless labor and brutal whippings in freezing cold, Douglass felt his intellectual spark extinguished: 'My natural elasticity was crushed, my intellect languished, the disposition to read departed, the cheerful spark that lingered about my eye died; the dark night of slavery closed in upon me; and behold a man transformed into a brute!'

The climax came on an August morning when Covey attempted to tie Douglass's legs in the barn to whip him. At that moment, Douglass resolved to defend himself. For two hours, he fought Covey hand-to-hand with ferocious strength, seizing him by the throat and flinging him into the manure. Covey never struck him again. Although legally still a slave, Douglass was spiritually reborn: 'This battle with Mr. Covey was the turning-point in my career as a slave. It rekindled the few expiring embers of freedom, and revived within me a sense of my own manhood. It was a glorious resurrection, from the tomb of slavery, to the heaven of freedom.'
